A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to altered mental status and trouble with walking.  She has a history of parkinsonism and has had increased difficulty ambulating over the past few days.  The patient lives alone and has had a few minor falls recently.  Blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg and pulse is 68/min.  CT scan of the head is shown below.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌

options.text: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery

options.label: E
options.text: Rupture of the posterior communicating artery

explanation:
This patient's CT scan shows a crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdensity consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH), an accumulation of blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater that results from rupture of the bridging cortical veins (drain blood from cerebral cortex into dural venous sinuses).

SDH characteristically occurs in elderly patients following minor trauma.  With advancing age, progressive cerebral atrophy increases the distance between the brain surface and the overlying skull, placing the bridging veins under greater tension and making them prone to tearing.  Other vulnerable populations include patients with neurodegenerative disorders (eg, parkinsonism), those with alcohol use disorder, and infants (eg, shaken baby syndrome).

Because the source of bleeding is venous, hemorrhage accumulates slowly, producing a gradual rise in intracranial pressure and a correspondingly insidious clinical course.  Symptoms may evolve over days to weeks and include progressive headache, altered mental status, gait disturbance, and seizures. The presentation is often subtle and highly variable, earning SDH the designation of a "great imitator".

(Choices A and E)  The posterior communicating artery is the second most common site of berry aneurysms after the anterior communicating artery.  Rupture of these aneurysms results in subarachnoid bleeding that tracks along the basal cisterns and sulci, producing a star-shaped pattern.

(Choice C)  The lenticulostriate arteries arise from the middle cerebral arteries and supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia.  Hypertension can predispose to rupture of these vessels, resulting in intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

(Choice D)  Rupture of the middle meningeal artery causes an epidural hematoma, which classically presents with a brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval, then rapid neurologic deterioration as the high pressure arterial bleed expands.  Because the epidural space is tightly bound by dural adhesions at the cranial sutures, the hematoma forms a lens-shaped (biconvex) collection that does not cross suture lines, although it can cross the midline because it lies superficial to the dura.  In contrast, an SDH can cross suture lines but cannot cross the midline, which is occupied by the falx cerebri.

Educational objective:Subdural hematoma occurs due to rupture of the bridging cortical veins that traverse the subdural space.  It is common in elderly patients due to brain atrophy that stretches the veins and predisposes them to rupture.  Imaging shows a crescent-shaped mass that can cross suture lines but cannot cross the midline.​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌
